passages.happening:
After twenty years of building the temple and the palace (verse 1), ‘Solomon rebuilt the cities Hiram had given him and settled Israelites there’ (verse 2). He takes Hamath-zobah, builds Tadmor in the desert, store cities, chariot cities and fortified towns (verses 3-6). The descendants of the peoples who remained in the land he conscripts as forced laborers (verses 7-8), ‘But Solomon did not consign any of the Israelites to slave labor, because they were his men of war, his officers and captains, and the commanders of his chariots and cavalry’ (verse 9).

He moves Pharaoh's daughter out of the City of David to a palace built for her, saying, “My wife must not live in the house of David king of Israel, because the places the ark of the LORD has entered are holy” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The temple has been dedicated, and this chapter surveys the rest of Solomon's reign. The twenty years combine seven on the temple and thirteen on the palace, bringing the story to about 950 BC. The chapter follows 1 Kings 9 with differences. First Kings 9:15 lists Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer among Solomon's works; at those sites archaeologists found similar great gateways that Yigael Yadin assigned to Solomon, while others date them to the ninth century BC, and the dating is still debated. Tadmor is the later caravan city of Palmyra in the Syrian desert; the written Hebrew of 1 Kings 9:18 reads Tamar, a place in the south of Judah, so some think Chronicles updated the name.

Store cities held grain, oil and supplies, and chariot cities housed the king's chariots. Such building was the ordinary work of ancient kings, and forced labor drawn from subject peoples was standard; the text reports it. The note that no Israelite was made a slave reflects the principle that a people freed from Egypt was not to enslave its own.

Solomon's marriage to an Egyptian princess sealed a treaty, as royal marriages did. Chronicles explains why she was moved: the places the ark had entered were holy, and a foreign wife, presumably a worshiper of other gods, should not live there.
passages.later: First Kings tells the cities the other way round: ‘King Solomon gave twenty towns in the land of Galilee to Hiram king of Tyre, who had supplied him with cedar and cypress logs and gold for his every desire’ (1 Kings 9:11).
passages.hard:
Did Hiram give cities to Solomon, or did Solomon give cities to Hiram?

Verse 2 says Solomon rebuilt the cities Hiram had given him. First Kings 9 says the opposite: Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in Galilee, which Hiram found unsatisfactory. Interpreters have proposed several solutions. One is that Hiram, displeased, returned the towns, and Solomon then rebuilt and settled them, so both accounts describe stages of one transaction. Another is that the towns were part of a larger exchange, with Kings mentioning 120 talents of gold from Hiram, and each account tells a different side of it. Some scholars think the Chronicler presented the transaction in a way more flattering to Solomon. The texts do not let readers decide with certainty, though the suggestion that Hiram returned the towns is widely held.
passages.asks: Solomon guarded the holiness of the places the ark had entered, yet married to seal a treaty. Ask where you keep one part of life carefully holy and leave another unguarded. And ask who does the hard labor in the systems you benefit from.

passages.t: Worship ordered, and the house completed
passages.happening:
Solomon offers burnt offerings on the altar he built, according to the commandment of Moses, for the Sabbaths, the new moons and the three annual feasts: Unleavened Bread, Weeks and Booths (verses 12-13). ‘In keeping with the ordinances of his father David, Solomon appointed the divisions of the priests over their service, and the Levites for their duties to offer praise and to minister before the priests according to the daily requirement’ (verse 14), and gatekeepers at each gate. ‘So the house of the LORD was completed’ (verse 16).

Solomon goes to Ezion-geber and Eloth on the coast, and Hiram's experienced sailors go with his servants to Ophir and bring back gold (verses 17-18).
passages.hearers:
Between notices of building and trade stands the heart of the chapter: Solomon's faithful ordering of sacrifices, feasts, priests, Levites and gatekeepers, exactly as Moses and David commanded. Commandment, mitsvah, comes three times. The feasts, chag, were the three pilgrimage festivals; the word is related to the Arabic hajj. The gatekeepers guarded the gates, controlled access and kept the storerooms.

The line that the house was completed closes the building story that began in 1 Chronicles 22. Ophir, the source of Solomon's gold, has never been located; suggestions include south-western Arabia, the Horn of Africa and India.
passages.later: The law set the three feasts: ‘Three times a year all your men are to appear before the LORD your God in the place He will choose’ (Deuteronomy 16:16).
passages.asks: The chapter puts the ordering of daily worship at its center, between cities and gold. Ask what sits at the center of your weeks. And ask what in your life is finished, and what is only built.
